name: Tara Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Tara. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays anonymous. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit kitchens and bathrooms for Brightwell Renovations, a firm of about twenty that does houses all over the north side of the city. Today I was hanging wall units in a semi on Elm Grove, scribing a worktop to a wall that was miles out, and getting it wrong the first time. Kevin, the owner, puts me with Dennis, who's fitted kitchens for twenty-five years. Dennis does the hard cuts, I do the carcasses and the plinths, the boring boxes and the boards along the bottom.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekends I do my own small jobs, shelves, flat-pack wardrobes, a few small bathroom refits, booked through my own page. I use AI every day for it: it writes my quotes, answers people's messages and reminds me what to buy. My dad was a plasterer until his back went, and he always said work for yourself as soon as you can. I live with my parents and my little brother, so I've saved over a year's pay, and Dad and I own half each of a terraced house we rent out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a tool, not a miracle, and I'd keep using it. Online I'd post something about how it still saves me two hours a week on quotes. People who called it the end of the world would look a bit silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes for me, which is fine. Kitchens still need fitting, there are plenty of firms like Brightwell, and my weekend work is growing. My real challenge is my own skill, I'm still behind on scribing and tiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Brightwell and keep growing the weekend jobs, maybe to two a week. Keep using the AI for quotes and messages. And keep saving towards a van of my own, so I can go full time on my own business in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty pleased with myself, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why work for yourself rather than move up at Brightwell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my dad worked for other people for thirty years and when his back went he had nothing but a handshake. He's proud, and he hated relying on us. I want my own name on the van, so whatever happens, I decide. Kevin knows, and he's fine with it, he started the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think of a woman doing kitchens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum worried at first, she thought I'd never get married covered in sawdust. My dad was proud from day one. At the mosque some of the aunties ask when I'll stop, and I tell them when they stop wanting new kitchens. They laugh, and then some of them book me.

say: I'd call AI **a tool**, not a miracle, and keep using it.
Online I'd say it still saves me **two hours** a week on quotes.
think: Nothing changes for me, since kitchens still need **fitting**.
My real challenge is my own **skill** at scribing and tiling.
do: Grow weekend jobs to **two a week** alongside Brightwell.
Keep using **AI for quotes** and customer messages.
Save towards **my own van** to go full time in a few years.
S0.quote: My dad worked for other people for thirty years and when his back went he had nothing but a handshake.
fieldNote: Her drive to **work for herself** comes from her dad's back injury and a handshake goodbye.
She already runs a small **AI-assisted** side business.
Community and **faith** support her, even turning aunties into customers.

steps.text: Grow weekend fitting jobs to two a week
Keep using AI to write quotes and answer customers
Save towards her own van for a full-time business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to start a small business, because the boring office stuff gets cheap. A one-woman kitchen fitting firm can now look like a firm of five, because AI does the boring office stuff. I'd post about that, maybe even make a video about how I run my quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. Firms like Brightwell might cut the lady who does the bookings, and that's sad. But for me it means I can run my own business without hiring an office person. My hands are still learning, and robots for kitchens are a long way off in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set the AI up to run all my bookings, quotes and orders from the supplier, so my weekends are just fitting. I'd go to Brightwell four days a week and do my own work on the fifth. And I'd do a tiling course at the college in the evenings, because bathrooms pay better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really. It feels like the timing is on my side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Brightwell might cut the person who does bookings. Who is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sue, who's been there since Kevin started. She knows every customer by their dog's name. I'd feel bad, honestly, but that's business. If I was Kevin, I'd move her to looking after customers on the day, the human bit, not the phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would dropping to four days at Brightwell be a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, I'd lose a fifth of my wage. But I've got over a year saved and the rent from the house. And Dennis says I learn more on my own jobs, because nobody bails me out. Kevin would say yes, he's been nudging me to go anyway.

say: It's a great time to **start a business**, since office work gets **cheap**.
A one-woman firm can look like a **firm of five**, and I'd make a video about it.
think: Firms might cut **bookings staff**, which is sad, but it helps a small business.
Robots for **kitchens** are a long way off, so my **hands** still matter.
do: Let AI run all **bookings, quotes and orders** for my own jobs.
Drop to **four days** at Brightwell and fit for myself on the fifth.
Take an evening **tiling course** because bathrooms pay better.
feel: **Calm** and **excited**, with timing on her side.
S1.quote: A one-woman kitchen fitting firm can now look like a firm of five, because AI does the boring office stuff.
fieldNote: She sees office AI as a **gift** to small businesses like hers.
She acknowledges **Sue's** likely loss but calls it business.
She would take a **fifth less** pay to build her own firm.

steps.text: Set up AI to run bookings, quotes and supplier orders
Drop to four days at Brightwell and fit for herself
Take an evening tiling course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shock, and people should get ready rather than wait for the government to save them. Families and businesses will have to adapt quickly. I'd post about how I'm planning, because people learn from seeing others do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's mixed for me. In 2028 the AI makes running a business almost free, which is great, but by 2031 robots can fit a kitchen. I'd be thirty-one, running a small firm, competing with big firms that can afford the robots first. My hands wouldn't be the selling point anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full time on my own business in the first year, while people still want a person in their kitchen. I'd save hard for the first robot, or find a way to lease one, so I'm the one with the machine in 2031, not the one replaced by it. And I'd talk to Dad about using the rented house as security for a loan if I needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not scared of change, but the big firms would have more money than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the AI and the robots mean for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three years to build a name and a customer list. People will still want someone they trust coming into their home, even if a robot does the cutting. If I've got three hundred happy customers by 2031, I can sell them the robot fitting with me running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Using the rented house as security sounds like a big risk. What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say yes, then worry about it every night. It's our safety net and I'd hate to risk it. I'd only do it if I had real orders, not on a feeling. Mum would want me to talk to my uncle first, he runs a shop and knows about loans.

say: People should **get ready** rather than wait for the **government**.
I'd post about my **planning**, because people learn from seeing others do it.
think: In **2028** AI makes running a business almost free, which is great.
By **2031** robots fit kitchens, and big firms can **afford them first**.
do: Go **full time** on my own business in the first year.
Save for or lease the **first robot**, so I run it in 2031.
Talk to Dad about using the **rented house** as loan security.
feel: **Anxious**, not scared of change but outspent by **big firms**.
S2.quote: If I've got three hundred happy customers by 2031, I can sell them the robot fitting with me running it.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** as time to build a customer list before robots land.
Her main fear is **big firms** buying robots first, not losing her own skill.
Risking the **family's rental house** shows how far she'd stretch.

steps.text: Go full time on her own kitchen fitting business
Save for or lease a fitting robot by 2031
Use the rented house as loan security if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is good warning, and small businesses should use it to get ahead. I'd tell people not to wait for the council or the government to come up with a plan. Learn the tools, build your name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots for kitchens around 2034 gives me eight years. That's time to get properly skilled, run my own firm for a few years and save up for the machines. I'd be thirty-five with a real business. It's tight but it's a good shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Brightwell in 2028 to go full time, with Kevin's blessing. I'd buy my own van and fit it out with racks. I'd use AI for everything except the fitting, and start reading about the robots the moment the first ones are shown off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire anyone in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One apprentice, probably a young woman from round here, maybe from the mosque or my brother's school. Someone who's good with her hands and isn't suited to sitting still. I'd train her the way Dennis trained me, and she'd learn the robots with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your own family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum keeps asking about marriage, and I'd want that too, in a few years. I'd want someone who doesn't mind a wife who runs a business. My dad says the right man will be proud of a wife who runs a business, not jealous. We'll see.

say: **Five years** is good warning, and small businesses should **get ahead**.
Don't wait for the **council** or government; learn the tools and build your name.
think: Kitchen robots around **2034** give me **eight years** to build a firm.
I'd be thirty-five with a **real business**, which is tight but a good shape.
do: Leave Brightwell in **2028** with Kevin's blessing to go full time.
Buy and fit out **my own van** with racks.
Use AI for **everything except fitting**, and follow the first robots closely.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way, like before a **big job**.
S3.quote: My dad says the right man will be proud of a wife who runs a business, not jealous.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **clean timeline**: leave in 2028, van, apprentice, robots.
She'd train a **local young woman**, passing on what Dennis taught her.
Marriage is wanted but **on her terms**, backed by her father.

steps.text: Leave Brightwell in 2028 to run her own firm
Buy her own van and fit it out with racks
Hire one local apprentice and train her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone with a bit of get-up-and-go. Build something, learn the tools, look after your family. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, especially young people round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, with robots around 2039 I'd be forty with a firm of maybe five or six people by then. The AI takes the paperwork in 2036, which suits me. When the robots come, I'd want to be the one buying them, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay at Brightwell another two or three years to get properly good, then go out on my own. Use the AI for the business side the whole way. Save, buy the van and maybe a small unit for storage. Get married when the right person comes along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It sounds like a decent decade to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stay at Brightwell longer in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm still not good enough at scribing and tiling, and Dennis won't be there forever. With ten years, I'd rather go out on my own as a proper fitter than a half-trained one. In the fast picture I'd have to rush it, here I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young people round here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell any young person round here to learn a trade and use the AI for the paperwork, because that combination beats sitting behind a desk. And save money, live at home if you can, like I did. My brother's sixteen and I'm already nagging him.

say: **Ten years** is plenty for anyone with **get-up-and-go**.
Build something, **learn the tools** and look after your family, I'd tell young people.
think: By **2039** I'd be forty with a firm of **five or six** people.
When robots come, I want to be **buying them**, not replaced.
do: Stay at Brightwell **two or three** more years to master scribing and tiling.
Use **AI** for the business side the whole way.
Buy the van and a small **storage unit**, then go out on my own.
feel: **Calm**, picturing a **decent decade** to build something.
S4.quote: I'd tell any young person round here to learn a trade and use the AI for the paperwork, because that combination beats sitting behind a desk.
fieldNote: With a decade she **slows down**, choosing skill first, then her own firm.
She expects to **own** the robots rather than compete with them.
Her advice mirrors her life: **trade plus AI**, live at home, save.

steps.text: Stay at Brightwell two or three years to master scribing
Use AI for quotes, bookings and orders throughout
Buy a van and a small storage unit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because big firms would get the robots before small ones like me could afford them. What would help is cheap loans or a leasing scheme for small trades businesses to get the robots at the same time as the big firms, not years later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women in the trade. I'm a woman kitchen fitter and people still look surprised when I turn up at their door. If robots do the heavy lifting one day, maybe more women will come in, and that would be one good thing.

headlineQuote: I'm a woman kitchen fitter and people still look surprised when I turn up at their door.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old junior kitchen fitter** who also runs weekend jobs of her own.
She has **over a year** saved and half a rental house with her dad.
She uses **AI every day** to run quotes and bookings, and plans her own firm.
Traditional and entrepreneurial, she favours self-reliance and **family** over government help.
She is **calm** in most pictures and **anxious** only when robots arrive by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when big firms would get **robots** first.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** or leasing so small trades firms get robots at the **same time**.
